barCharacter: The Narrator (Monster Prom). Its job is closest: the voice that undercuts every speaker and gets the last word, deadpan and never loud. Vera is the persona cousin (status queen with standards), but the corpus has only nine verbatim Vera lines. Her lines also beat ours on economy and show the core gap: Vera assumes her status, Vesper announces hers.

ours12: Nav, I muted the moon landing. I can mute you.
I got this letter by telegram, and replied stop.
You woke the trucker, Brock. He was doing so well.
Quill, I understood one word in four, and it was thou, and that's enough.
Don't talk with your mouth full. It carries. Sixty miles.
For Crumb, a lullaby, two minutes on medium, then nothing.
For Vex, a song with no chorus. It just stops. Like this.
Ten seconds of dead air, Prince, in your honour.
I've hung up on real princes, Prince, and they paid.
A navy flattered me in formation, and you're a dinghy.
Brock. You're too loud for my hours. I'm changing my hours.
You, Prince. I don't believe a word. I just like the stationery.
bar12: Does… Scott know any other people? Signs are pointing to "no."
It is just paper! Luckily Scott will believe anything.
Later, you see Damien packing a bag.
Liam vanishes in a cloud of mist and angst.
Later, you see Liam beaming to himself. Liam? Beaming?
You see Vera at the mirror, attempting to tame her hair with a cattle prod.
Whoa. You know this is a serious situation if it's causing Vera to show empathy.

headToHead.a_voice: Bar. Cover the names and the Narrator is identified by shape alone: second-person stage setup ('Later, you see...', 'You notice...'), then a clipped echo or undercut ('Liam? Beaming?'). Ours is identified by vocabulary: dead air, trucker, telegram, dedication, caller. Take those nouns out and 'Brock. You're too loud for my hours. I'm changing my hours.' or 'You, Prince. I don't believe a word. I just like the stationery.' could be Maximilian. Worse, eight of our twelve best are short stacked sentences, which is the one shape the persona forbids. Her written signature, one slow comma-and sentence with the verdict last, produces mostly the template lines and only a handful of winners ('it was thou, and that's enough').
headToHead.b_construction: Bar, narrowly. Ours is economical, and the telegram, trucker and lullaby lines turn cleanly on the last word. But the turn is predictable: in most of our lines the punchline is a legend she announces, so a viewer can see 'and you're a dinghy' coming from 'A navy flattered me'. The Narrator's turns come from looking at the other character (packing a bag, the cattle prod, the fans at maximum speed), so each one is new. 'Last man who pitched like that sold me the sea' and 'Satellites call me when they're lonely, and they're calmer' have turns that do not resolve.
headToHead.c_quotable: Bar. 'Liam vanishes in a cloud of mist and angst' and 'second-most dangerous day of school ever' are clip-and-share lines. Ours has two clippable lines (moon landing, telegram stop) and one strong one (trucker); the rest are pleasant in the moment and gone by the next episode.
headToHead.verdict: If both ran tonight, the Narrator is the better-written character. Vesper has a real world (the booth, the trucker, the switchboard) and four or five lines that would hold up, but her joke engine is visible by the third reaction.

templates: A: '[I did a legendary thing / a grand thing once did X to me], and you're [smaller].' About 50 lines across reacts, cardReacts, cuts, one-on-ones, questions, twists, intros and hold. This is the engine of the bank, and the 'and you' turn can be called from the first clause.
B: 'I never X, and [here I am doing X].' The charmed reaction, about 13 lines. Every time she is won over it is phrased as breaking a lifelong rule, so being charmed has one sound.
C: 'For [Name], a [record]. [Length]. [Tag].' Seven dedications in 32 cringe/cut slots. The persona asks for sparing use, and 'Both called Goodbye' is the title-says-the-insult it bans.

Recurring props worn thin: lighthouse 4 times, switchboard 5, trucker 4. On the nautical side: coast guard, sold me the sea, foghorn fleet, ships home, admirals, navy and dinghy, two oceans, pirate fishing boat, the tall mast, sinking ship, tide tables, gale warning (12 or more).
Three-short-sentence stack (the persona forbids it), about 25 lines. See ruleBreaks.
ruleBreaks: Word limits: no hard breach. Longest reveal: '{card}, and I'd have played that one twice, and I never play anything twice.' (14 words; the type sets no reveal cap, but every other short slot is capped at 12).
No em dashes, emoji, lists, therapy talk, 'as an AI', exclamation marks, real people or brands. All PG-13.
Ends on the banned filler 'lovely': 'You beat me to it, and I'd prepared something lovely.'

biggestGap: Vesper announces her status and the bar assumes it: about fifty lines are 'I [did a legendary thing], and you're [smaller]', so the brag is the punchline and the turn can be called from the first clause. In the next pass, keep the legend to at most one line per suitor. Rebuild the reacts, cardReacts and cuts so that the last words land on something specific the suitor just said or wears (the visor, the headset, the bucket helm, the floating), with her history either gone or taken for granted inside the sentence, the way Vera takes the murder cover-up for granted.

notes: Round 3, fresh eyes; only the page was judged. monster-prom-lines.md was present and read in full; charm-notes.md was skimmed. 191 lines were counted in the bank (intro, questions, react, cardReact, cut, twistIntro, ex, oneOnOne, hold, pick, reveal, outro). Generic share: 95 unique lines fall in at least one generic or template bucket, which is 50%. Template A alone is about 26% of the bank. On a 24/7 show, viewers will hear 'X did Y to me once, and you...' several times an episode. The persona instruction itself causes this ('status tossed off mid-sentence, at moon-landing size'). The writer applied it to nearly every line instead of using it as one move among several. A second structural problem: her signature slow comma-and sentence produces the template lines, while her best lines are clipped stacks that the persona forbids. The writer needs either to find winning lines in the long shape or to admit that the clipped shape is hers. Both are better than the current split. What works and should be extended: the reveal 'none' lines ('I left it out like a porch light. Nobody came.') and the slip lines ('Vex, nobody recommends a request line. You just find me at four a.m.') have a melancholy no rival on the cast has. That is the X-but-secretly-Y contrast the bar builds every character on, and it is currently buried under the brags.
